one_liner: Rust/WebAssembly single-page-app framework without a virtual DOM; its 2022 build runs the js-framework-benchmark about 1.5x faster than React 19.2 hooks.
what_it_does: Spair is a client-side UI framework for single-page applications written in Rust and compiled to wasm32-unknown-unknown. Views and components are plain Rust impl blocks marked with attribute macros (#[create_view], #[impl_component]) whose view() body describes the HTML in Rust call syntax; state lives in a Rust struct and event handlers are callbacks that mutate it. It is a different programming model from React, not a drop-in replacement, and has only basic routing, no SSR, no event delegation and no documentation beyond the examples directory.
how_it_is_fast: No virtual DOM: in the current main branch the proc macros work out at compile time which DOM nodes can change, build each view from an HtmlTemplateElement fragment clone, and on update write only those nodes. Keyed lists are reconciled by trimming the common prefix and suffix, detecting single forward or backward moves, and running a longest-increasing-subsequence pass (code copied from the axelf4/lis crate) on the middle so only rows outside the LIS are moved, keyed through an FxHashMap. The measured 0.0.8 design instead re-ran a render function that compared new values with cached ones in place, with static_nodes/static_attributes markers to skip parts that never change; the spair-qr variant adds queue render (QrVec/QrVal containers that push only the changed pieces), which is why it is faster on select (2.5 ms vs 3.7 ms).
when_to_use: You are already writing the front end in Rust/Wasm and want one of the faster Rust frameworks in krausest/js-framework-benchmark: spair-qr's geometric mean is 0.616x React's time and spair's is 0.662x, ahead of leptos 0.7.0 (0.684x), dominator (0.681x), dioxus 0.7.2 (0.698x), sycamore (0.711x), mogwai 0.6.5 (0.719x) and yew 0.23 (0.819x) in the same results.ts (derived from page data).
Keyed tables or lists where rows are reordered or swapped: swap rows is 12.5 ms against React's 89.7 ms, the largest single gap in the suite rows.
Large initial renders: create 10,000 rows 262.7 ms vs React 401.0 ms (but 1.23x vanilla JavaScript's 213.3 ms).
Pages where first paint and download size matter more than heap: first paint 137.3 ms vs 226.6 ms and 31.8 kB vs 51.4 kB brotli-compressed against React.
when_not_to_use: You need the fastest possible DOM updates: spair is slower than hand-written vanilla JavaScript on all 9 CPU rows (1.205x geometric-mean time) and slower than the suite's hand-written wasm-bindgen entry (0.584x React), and it is effectively tied with React on create 1,000 rows (24.6 vs 23.6 ms).
Memory-constrained pages: ready memory 1.70 MB vs React 1.19 MB, run memory 4.97 vs 4.37 MB, and memory after creating and clearing rows 3.54 vs 1.98 MB (spair-qr 2.99 MB).

Production apps that need a stable API, SSR, event delegation, real routing, documentation or a community: the README lists all of these as missing and the main branch was redesigned again in January 2026.
Sites with a strict Content Security Policy: the suite flags both spair entries with issue #1139 (Function/eval-style code in the generated bundle).
You want the benchmarked code: the numbers are for crates.io 0.0.8 (November 2022); the main branch (0.0.10, unpublished) is a complete redesign the README says has no benchmarks yet.

integration.dependencies: wasm-bindgen, js-sys, web-sys, wasm-bindgen-futures, log, rustc-hash, and the spair-macros proc-macro crate (syn 2, quote, proc-macro2); examples are built with Trunk
integration.min_toolchain: main branch uses Rust edition 2024 (Rust 1.85 or newer) with the wasm32-unknown-unknown target; the benchmarked 0.0.8 crate's minimum is not documented
integration.platforms: Browsers only (wasm32-unknown-unknown with web-sys DOM bindings); tests run under wasm-pack test --headless --firefox
integration.thread_safety: not documented; it runs on the browser main thread and components are single-threaded (Rc-based component handles)

gotchas: The published crate and the benchmark lag the repository: crates.io stops at 0.0.9 (2022-11-20) and the js-framework-benchmark entry pins 0.0.8, while main is an unpublished 0.0.10 rewrite with a different macro API, so code written from the current README will not match either the crate or the measured build.

The benchmark bundle is prebuilt: build-prod is a no-op that serves the checked-in Trunk output last rebuilt by the author on 2022-11-19, so the Rust and wasm-bindgen versions behind the Chrome 154 numbers are those of late 2022 and are not recorded.

The view syntax depends on attribute macros rewriting Rust code that looks like function calls; the README warns this 'is a kind of abusing Rust, and may become invalid by changes in Rust in the future'. HTML names that clash with Rust keywords need raw identifiers (r#type, r#for).

The spair-qr benchmark's swap handler calls swap(1, 998).unwrap_throw() without the bounds guard the plain spair version has, so it throws if fewer than 999 rows exist; this does not affect the suite's 1,000-row runs but shows the queue-render API returns errors the caller must handle.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the Rust/Wasm siblings measured by the same suite, pick spair (preferably its queue-render mode) over mogwai when keyed-list update speed is the deciding factor (0.616-0.662x React vs mogwai's 0.719x); pick mogwai or the more established Rust frameworks when you need a published, documented API, since spair's fast build is a 2022 release and its current code is an unbenchmarked rewrite.
verified_claims_summary: In krausest/js-framework-benchmark (WebDriver-driven Chrome 154.0.8037.98 on an Apple M4 MacBook Pro 14, a development snapshot), the author-submitted spair 0.0.8 keyed implementation's median total times give a geometric mean of 0.662x React 19.2 hooks over the nine CPU rows (spair-qr 0.616x), but 1.205x vanilla JavaScript (spair-qr 1.122x); medians recomputed from results.ts match the record (create 1,000 rows 24.6 vs 23.6 ms, swap 12.5 vs 89.7 ms, create 10,000 rows 262.7 vs 401.0 ms).
status_note: Single-author MPL-2.0 project still committed to in February 2026, but the actively developed main branch is an unpublished, undocumented rewrite while the benchmarked and published versions date from November 2022, so treat it as experimental rather than production-ready.
